title: Who holds the consent? How tokenization works without cards
summary: Learn how payment tokenization works without cards in Asia: why e-wallet and direct debit tokens are stored consent, and why they stay with one PSP. The post Who holds the consent? How tokenization works without cards appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
Many global merchants operate with the idea that recurring-payments playbooks start with the card. Store it as a token, charge it again for renewals and top-ups, and route that token to whichever processor offers the best price. In the US and Europe, where most customers have a card, that approach has worked for decades.


Across Asia however, many customers would rather pay from an e-wallet or via bank transfer. In this region, the card playbook rests on two assumptions: that customer has a card to store, and that stored token works with any processor.


Tokenization still exists on e-wallets and bank transfers. Without a card number underneath, though, what the merchant stores is the customer's consent to be charged. That changes who controls the token, and where it can be used.


## **Pull or push decides what can be tokenized**


Southeast Asian shoppers pay in many ways, from QR codes to e-wallets and bank transfers, as our


[Xendit Ecommerce Payments Momentum Report 2026](https://www.xendit.co/en/ecomms-momentum-report/) shows. A QR code only starts the payment, though. When a customer scans QRIS in Indonesia or PromptPay QR in Thailand, they approve a one-time payment from their e-wallet or bank account, and nothing is left for the merchant to charge again. For recurring payments, the merchant needs the customer’s consent with that wallet or bank directly.


How money leaves the account decides the rest. In a pull payment, the customer authorizes once and the merchant collects later, as with a direct debit. In a push payment, the customer approves every transaction, as with a QR scan or a PromptPay transfer, so there is nothing to store. E-wallets generally support pull payments. Bank transfers come in both forms.


## **In an e-wallet, the auto-debit agreement is the token**


In Indonesia, 70% of online shoppers pay with e-wallets, according to[our ecommerce report](https://www.xendit.co/en/ecomms-momentum-report/) . The wallets that matter here hold the customer’s account, often with a stored balance: GoPay, OVO, DANA, and ShopeePay among others. Apple Pay and Google Pay usually work differently. In most markets, they wrap a card, which is tokenized like any other.


That makes a wallet the closest equivalent to a card on file. The customer signs an auto-debit authorization inside the wallet app, and the merchant receives a token it can charge for future renewals or top-ups.


Getting there takes more groundwork than cards. Wallet operators typically review a merchant’s use case and expected volumes before switching on auto-debit, and some offer a lighter tier where the customer still confirms each payment. Across Southeast Asia, Xendit supports e-wallet tokenization for GoPay in Indonesia, Touch ‘n Go in Malaysia, and GCash (through Link & Pay) and Maya in the Philippines.


## **On a bank account, no mandate means no token**


Direct debit is a pull payment. The customer signs a mandate once, and the merchant collects on a schedule. Banks in Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines offer it, and the mandate is the token. Not every linked account lets the merchant collect alone, though. In the Philippines, several banks' direct debit links can be stored for repeat use, but the customer still approves each payment.


Real-time payments are push payments. UPI in India, PromptPay in Thailand, PayNow in Singapore and DuitNow in Malaysia move money instantly from a banking app, and 61% of Thai online shoppers prefer bank transfers. Each payment is a one-time push, so on its own there is nothing to tokenize. Recurring payments need a mandate layer on top, as India built with UPI AutoPay, and that mandate becomes the token.


The rule is simple: no standing mandate, no token.


## **Non-card tokens stay with the processor that enrolled them**


The second assumption fails next. A card token can be passed to several payment service providers (PSPs) and routed for the best price, because card networks vouch for any authorized acquirer.


Non-card tokens don't travel. An e-wallet token is issued to the PSP that enrolled the agreement, and to the wallet, any other PSP has no authorization on file. A bank mandate is tied the same way to the one processor that set it up. Adding or switching providers means asking customers for their consent again.


Fixing this would take a neutral layer above the PSPs, with a shared registry of tokens and mandates and agreed rules on liability. Almost no one is building it yet.


## **Plan for the consent you can't move**


Until then, merchants can build much of the outcome themselves:


1. **Own the system of record.** Map each customer to their per-PSP mandates in your own orchestration layer, so the portability lives with you.


2. **Pre-enroll with a second PSP where the rail allows it.** It costs an extra consent step, which good UX can make feel routine.


3. **Keep the consent context,** so a lapsed mandate becomes a one-tap re-authorization instead of silent churn.


4. **Keep a backup payment method on file.**[Xendit Subscriptions](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/recurring/) lets merchants attach up to five payment methods to one plan, so a failed charge on one falls back to the next.


The choice of payments partner matters here too. A partner with


[direct connections to local wallets and banks](https://www.xendit.co/en/company/xendit-licenses/) knows which methods in each market support full auto-debit and which only store a link, and can set up enrollment so customers aren't asked twice. Xendit brings


[local e-wallets, direct debit, cards and QR](https://xendit.co/en-id/products/all-payment-methods/) together in one integration.


## **Start with who holds the consent**


Across Asia, tokenization lives on as stored consent. It exists only where a merchant can pull under a standing mandate, and it stays with the processor that enrolled it.


For merchants planning recurring payments in Asia, the question to ask of each payment method is who holds the consent, and whether anyone can pull against it. If you're working through that for Southeast Asia,


[our team can help](https://www.xendit.co/en/contact/) you map which local methods support tokenization in each market.
